milestones.title: Vietnamese customs post at Khmer Prey Nokor
milestones.detail: The Khmer king Chey Chettha II allowed Vietnamese settlers into the port of Prey Nokor, which they called Sài Gòn, and let the Nguyễn lords set up a customs house there.
milestones.source: Vo, Dang & Ho (2008), The Women of Vietnam, via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Names_of_Ho_Chi_Minh_City

milestones.title: Chinese Ming refugees allowed to settle
milestones.detail: Lord Nguyễn Phúc Tần let groups of Chinese refugees from the Qing conquest settle at Mỹ Tho, Biên Hòa and Saigon, the beginning of the Chinese trading community later centred on Cholon.

milestones.title: Nguyễn Hữu Cảnh establishes Vietnamese rule
milestones.detail: Sent south by the Nguyễn lords, Nguyễn Hữu Cảnh set up Vietnamese administration in the area, detaching it from Cambodia. This is the date Vietnam treats as the city's founding.

milestones.title: Chinese merchants move in; Cholon takes shape
milestones.detail: After fighting in 1776 destroyed their settlement at Cù lao Phố (Biên Hòa), Chinese merchants resettled beside Saigon and built the market that gave Chợ Lớn ('big market') its name.

milestones.title: Gia Định citadel built
milestones.detail: Two years after Nguyễn Ánh took the town, a Vauban-style citadel (Thành Bát Quái) was built with French engineers, making Gia Định his capital in the war against the Tây Sơn.

milestones.title: Citadel razed after the Lê Văn Khôi revolt
milestones.detail: Emperor Minh Mạng had the citadel dismantled after the revolt of 1833-35 and built a smaller one, Phụng Thành, in 1836.

milestones.title: French and Spanish forces capture Saigon
milestones.detail: A Franco-Spanish expedition took the town in 1859 and destroyed the citadel.

milestones.title: Treaty of Saigon cedes the city to France
milestones.detail: The treaty signed on 5 June 1862 ceded Saigon and the surrounding provinces. The French replanned it as the capital of the colony of Cochinchina.

milestones.title: Saigon and Cholon joined in one region
milestones.detail: On 27 April 1931 the two neighbouring municipalities, whose built-up areas had met by 1930, were combined as the Saigon-Cholon region.

milestones.title: Capital of the State of Vietnam
milestones.detail: On 14 June 1949 Bảo Đại made Saigon the capital of the State of Vietnam; from 1955 it was the capital of the Republic of Vietnam.

milestones.title: Tet Offensive
milestones.detail: Communist forces attacked the city during the 1968 Tet Offensive but failed to capture it. The population reached 3.3 million by 1970.

milestones.title: Fall of Saigon
milestones.detail: The city was captured on 30 April 1975, ending the Vietnam War.

milestones.title: Renamed Ho Chi Minh City
milestones.detail: In July 1976 Saigon (including Cholon), Gia Định province and two neighbouring districts were combined as Ho Chi Minh City, covering 1,295.5 km².

milestones.title: Landmark 81 completed
milestones.detail: The 461.2 m Landmark 81 tower in Bình Thạnh was completed, the tallest building in Vietnam.

milestones.title: Metro Line 1 opens
milestones.detail: The city's first metro line, 19.7 km from Bến Thành Market to the New Eastern Bus Terminus, opened on 22 December 2024.

milestones.title: Merger with Bình Dương and Bà Rịa-Vũng Tàu
milestones.detail: The two neighbouring provinces were merged into Ho Chi Minh City in 2025, greatly enlarging the municipality.

landmarks.name: Gia Định Citadel (Thành Bát Quái)
landmarks.note: Wall height given as 15 Vietnamese thước (4.8 m). Dismantled in 1835; its smaller replacement was destroyed by the French in 1859.

landmarks.name: Notre-Dame Cathedral Basilica of Saigon
landmarks.note: The two bell-tower spires were added in 1895 to the earlier cathedral; towers 57.6 m, 60.5 m to the top of the crosses.

landmarks.name: Tân Định Church
landmarks.note: The church dates from 1896-98; the 52.6 m bell tower was added in the 1928-29 renovation.

landmarks.name: Giác Lâm Temple stupa
landmarks.note: Seven-storey relic stupa begun in 1970 and inaugurated on 17 June 1994. Coordinates are those of the temple.

landmarks.name: Phú Mỹ Bridge
landmarks.note: Height of the main towers; opened 9 September 2009.

landmarks.name: Ba Son Bridge
landmarks.note: Height of the pylon; opened 28 April 2022.

notes: Start date is contested. 1623, when the Khmer king allowed a Vietnamese customs post at Prey Nokor, is the earliest dated record of the settlement and is used here. Vietnam officially dates the city from 1698, when Nguyễn Hữu Cảnh set up Vietnamese administration. Prey Nokor was a Khmer port before 1623, and Wikipedia mentions a 4th-century Funan temple and an 11th-century Cham settlement called Baigaur on the site, but none of these has a securely dated founding. Vietnamese Wikipedia notes that the name Sài Gòn first referred to the Chinese quarter around today's Cholon; the historic core is placed at the 1790 citadel, the centre of the Vietnamese and later French town. Population: no figure before 1800 was found (Vietnamese Wikipedia mentions 'over ten thousand' in the 18th century and 20,000-30,000 around 1772, without usable sources), and the 19th century rests on three estimates of uncertain coverage. From 1911 the series is for the agglomeration of Saigon plus Cholon, which were separate municipalities until 1931; figures for Saigon alone are much smaller (33,000 in 1897, 54,745 in 1905, 64,845 in 1911, 67,000 in 1913) and are not mixed in. Colonial counts are unreliable: the Hitotsubashi paper warns that migrant workers were under-registered, and sources disagree widely on Cholon (Vietnamese Wikipedia gives 63,237 for 1901 and 93,949 at the census of 15 February 1920, Britannica 1911 gives about 138,000 for 1907, while the official yearbooks give 181,000-191,655 for 1911-1919), probably because of different boundaries. Mitchell's 256,000 for both 1930 and 1940 (also quoted on Wikipedia for 1930) conflicts with the 1926 and 1939 counts and was left out, as were Mitchell's 182,000 (1910) and 180,000 (1920). The census results of 1921, 1931, 1936 and 1943 for the two towns could not be reached (the IRD paper by Gubry that tabulates them was unavailable). Landmarks: City Hall, the Opera House, the Central Post Office, Bến Thành Market, Vĩnh Nghiêm Pagoda, the Thiên Hậu and Jade Emperor temples and the Norodom Palace were left out because no sourced height was found. Tower heights, years and coordinates are from the CTBUH Skyscraper Center city listing; other coordinates are from Wikipedia.
